jane (acct-team): FYI — Acct Team received a red flag from a customer (tenant: acme-44). They send short chat completions in bursts (~40 reqs/s for 10s) and see 200ms normally but during a burst they get a lot of 3s+ tails and occasional 429s. They think Redwood is throttling them. They've given a sample request id: rq_3b9f2e and headers.

mina (support): Sorry they're hitting this. Can you paste the raw response / headers they saw? Also which endpoint (chat/generate/embeddings) and whether they use streaming or blocking?

jane (acct-team): Chat completions, non-streaming. Sample response they included: ````json
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/json
X-Request-Id: rq_3b9f2e
X-RateLimit-Limit: 600
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 167
{
  "error": {"message":"quota_exhausted: per_minute_limit","code":"rate_limited"}
}
````
They also sent a client-side timing trace: normal single requests ~150ms, but in the burst window median jumps to ~900ms and p95 ~3.2s.

oncall-bot: ALERT: burst_policy_triggered tenant=acme-44 policy=per_tenant_burst limit=40s window=60s

ben (sre): Two quick thoughts: (1) The 429 and X-RateLimit-Remaining=0 look like hitting a per-tenant quota bucket rather than an infra-level short-term throttle. (2) The latency spikes could be from continuous batching — small requests may wait for batch windows and then occasionally get a slow path (large KV cache miss / quantized path) that blocks the batch.

mina (support): Steps I've asked customer to run: (A) return the full headers for multiple failures (we need x-total-batch-time, x-inflight, x-kv-hit if they have it). (B) try a low-concurrency run (10 reqs/s) to confirm it's burst-dependent. (C) reproduce with a short script we gave.

eli (eng-runtime): Adding context from runtime: we have two interacting levers here — rate/quota enforcement and continuous batching + KV cache. If a tenant exhausts its minute quota, subsequent requests get 429s. But batching can amplify perceived throttling: when many tiny requests are in-flight, they are queued into batches (batch_window default ~20ms). If a batch encounters a KV cache miss (prefix not cached), that shard will do heavier work and increase tail latency for all requests in that batch (head-of-line blocking). That makes clients retry or pile on more requests, which can empty their per-minute bucket faster.

ben (sre): Repro steps for us: 1) From prod logs filter X-Request-Id rq_3b9f2e and surrounding minute. 2) Check tenant quota usage metrics (per_minute_consumed) and per-route throttle events. 3) Check runtime metrics: batch_queue_length, batch_exec_ms histogram, kv_cache_hit_rate by model+tenant, and per-shard CPU/GPU_exec_ms.

mina (support): Customer ran the script and attached a short trace. They also said reducing client concurrency reduces 429s but latency still has occasional 1-2s spikes.

eli (eng-runtime): That matches a mixed cause: quota exhaustion for sustained bursts + occasional slow-path batch due to KV cache miss or a quantized kernel fallback. Quick experiments we can run: - Short-term: increase tenant burst_tokens or per-minute quota for acme-44 so they can absorb burst. - Runtime tweak: lower batch_window_ms to 5ms for their route (reduces batching opportunity but reduces head-of-line effects). - Longer term: make batch scheduling preemptible for slow-paths or add per-request prefer_fast_path flag that bypasses quantized fallback.

ben (sre): Also verify customer client respects Retry-After and uses jittered backoff instead of tight immediate retries. Tight retries worsen bucket burn. Ask them to check their client is not re-sending identical requests on 429.

mina (support): I suggested the following immediate mitigation to customer: enable 'burst_extension' for their tenant (temp +1.5x minute quota) and patch their client to add exponential backoff with jitter. I also told them we might change batch_window for their route during the investigation. They asked for concrete repro commands so they can help us — suggested this local repro: ````bash
# simulate burst of 40 concurrent small requests
for i in $(seq 1 200); do
  curl -sS -X POST "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat" -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
    -d '{"model":"open-bison-7b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}' &
  if (( i % 40 == 0 )); then wait; fi
done
````
They can also use hey/fortio to generate RPS.

eli (eng-runtime): For eng action items: 1) check for any recent changes to kv_cache eviction TTLs or cache size that would cause lower hit rate for acme-44. 2) inspect batch histograms around rq_3b9f2e: any batches with single long tail (>1.5s)? If so, correlate with model kernel selection logs (we have flags when fallback to slow kernel occurs). 3) instrument and add x-kv-hit and x-batch-size headers in debug to help support triage.

ben (sre): I'll pull tenant quota ingestion logs + rate-limiter debug across the minute window. If quota was exhausted legitimately we should see per-minute_consumed spike and 429s aligning. If not, we might have a bug where fast retries are double-counted or a leak in bucket accounting.

mina (support): Customer accepted the temporary burst increase and will run another test in ~30m and send logs. For now I've scheduled a 1hr follow-up. If quick checks show kernel fallbacks or kv_hit drop we'll escalate to eng-runtime for a patch.

jane (acct-team): Thanks everyone — please post results here. Customer is quite sensitive to uptime; they'd prefer config tweaks over a long change.

eli (eng-runtime): Quick note for remediation playbook (internal): - Short-term: grant temporary burst_tokens and reduce server-side batch_window for that tenant. - Mid-term: add per-route 'latency_priority' flag which disables large-batch/quantized fallback for low-latency customers. - Observability: surface kv_cache_hit_rate and batch_latency in customer console + add alert for when p95 batch_exec_ms > 800ms.

mina (support): I'll update the ticket with these options and the repro script. Leaving this thread open until customer verifies the test results. :thumbsup:
